speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: DRYDOCKING OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE SHIPS AT UNITED STATES PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Railways and Canals. My attention has been called to the fact that the steamer Canadian Highlander of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine has been dry-docked and repaired in an American shipyard, and it is also proposed to have similar work done on the steamer Canadian Britisher. My
fMr. Marcil.l
question is: Why is this work not being performed in the shipyards at Halifax or Saint John?

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: DRYDOCKING OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT MERCHANT MARINE SHIPS AT UNITED STATES PORTS
speechtext:
Or Quebec?
Hon. R. J. MANIOlN (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, this matter was drawn to my attention by the hon. member and also by telegrams from a couple of gentlemen interested in the question both from the standpoint of the Canadian dry-docks and the standpoint of the eastern section of Canada. I made inquiries, because I was rather shocked to receive the messages. However, I am informed by the management of the Canadian National Railways, who are also, of course, the management of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, that it has always been their practice to have these ships repaired in the Canadian dry docks. At the present time they state however that both the drydock at Saint John and that at Halifax are tied up; they are occupied until dates beyond those which would suit the sailings of these ships. Full cargoes for Australia and Neiw Zealand are ordered for these ships, and those sending the cargoes insist, of course, that they leave on the scheduled date.
Perhaps the best procedure would be to read the telegram sent me by Mr. Fullerton, but I have given in brief the answer made by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I sent to Mr. Fullerton copies of the telegrams I had received, and I had asked him for an explanation. We felt, naturally, that in these days of unemployment the Canadian shipyards should be occupied, unless there was some very good reason to the contrary. His reply dated yesterday, from the city of Montreal, is as follows:
Your telegram of this date. Canadian Highlander was put into dry dock at New York which is port of call for this ship-
The Canadian Highlander is the first of the ships to which the hon. member referred. The telegram continues:
-for two days for survey and underwater painting on account of dry dock at Halifax which is her home port and the only Canadian port at which she calls being occupied until end! of April. Britisher will arrive new York-
This is the other ship to which reference was made-
-on 22nd and requires Canadian government survey, this voyage which will involve docking for twenty-four hours. Our Cornwallis goes in dock Saint John 25th for annual survey and repairs, and dry dock cannot take Britisher until 27th which is too late as she is scheduled

Waterloo, Qae., Post Office
to sail from Halifax on 28th and it is imperative that she leave earliest possible date. I am advised that this is first occasion in five years that any of our ships have been dry docked at an American port. This situation arises due to fact that eastern Canadian Atlantic dry docks filled to capacity. Owing to increased volume of exports to Australia and New Zealand and numerous requests from Canadian exporters for prompt dispatch, these vessels must remain as near to schedule dates as possible. It is of course our settled policy to give all of our repair work to Canadian dry docks.
C. P. Fullerton.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: WATERLOO, QUE., POST OFFICE PRESS REFERENCES TO ELECTORAL STANDARDS AND POLITICAL METHODS BASED ON FINDINGS OF MR. JUSTICE FOREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called may I refer to three articles appearing in the press, to which my attention has been draiwn and which refer to the administration of the Department of Public Works.
One is in the Montreal Gazette of March 21, 1935, and the heading is "Public men flayed in judge's report-Commissioner finds electoral standards in Shefford county depraved-Deserve ban of opinion-Mr. Justice Forest raps former MP. and ML.A. in report on Waterloo post office."
Another appeared in the Montreal Star of March 20, .1935, headed as follows, "Federal and provincial politicians in scandal-Ernest
Post Office Department

Boivin, former M.P. for Shefford, and Robert Bachand, M.L.A. for riding, roundly castigated by Mr. Justice Forest."
The other is in the Ottawa Journal of this morning, and is headed, " Judge denounces acts in building new post office-Says electoral standards at Waterloo and Granby, Quebec, ' absolutely depraved.' "
Then follow quotations from the report of Mr. Justice Forest. I think I should make to the house at this time a brief statement in connection with this matter.
At the earnest request of the present member for Shefford (Mr. Tetreault) an order in council was passed authorizing Mr. Justice Forest to investigate certain charges or allegations in connection with the acquiring of a site and the building of a post office at Waterloo. Mr. Justice Forest was appointed a commissioner to investigate these matters under the provisions of chapter 99, RB.C., the Inquiries Act. His report is dated February 8, 1935. It was translated and forwarded to the Justice department for such action as might appear proper in view of the statements contained in the report.
The articles in the press give no indication as to the date when the post office was constructed or these sites acquired. The sites were acquired in September, 1925, and October, 1927, and the building was completed in the year 1929. I think it proper under the circumstances to table a copy of the report both in English and French.

That will foe satisfactory. I should like to have these figures because so many conflicting statements have been made With regard to the amount of relief given, that I think a definite statement should be made showing the number of persons on relief on the first of January each year for the last five years. It would be very useful. I wish to discuss briefly the question of relief from the standpoint of the municipalities. During yesterday's discussion on the second reading several hon. members appealed to the government to come to the assistance of the municipalities more generously than during the past twelve months. I do not think there is any doubt that the responsibility which is being undertaken by the municipalities throughout Canada to-day is bringing many of them and some of the provinces as well to the verge of bankruptcy, and they cannot any longer carry the load. We see what is taking place in the urban centres. Montreal is compelled to go to the legislature for power to impose new forms of taxation, which will no doulbt be onerous to a large section of the
poorer people in that city. In Winnipeg the municipal authority has gone to the legislature seeking methods of imposing taxation upon those who are capable, in their opinion, of bearing an additional burden, and the move is being met with strenuous opposition by people who would be the last to object to carrying a share of the load in maintaining the unemployed. In British Columbia we see the city of Vancouver compelled, through circumstances over which the municipalities have no control, to do something to curb expenditures, and they are reducing interest on bonded indebtedness. I believe that the burden created last year by the present government in reducing grants to the provincial governments has placed a most unfair load on the municipal authorities. I do not think there is excuse for the action of the government in giving a fixed sum to the provincial governments, who in turn must reduce their grants to the municipalities. So far as Winnipeg was concerned it meant one of two things; either they had to reduce the amount of assistance given to those out of work or they had to impose additional taxation. They chose both; they made a reduction in the way of relief and also imposed further taxation ou the people. Yesterday the Minister of Labour, in a very apologetic and moderate speech-except for one part, where he said he would like to hang a few dozen people if he had the opportunity-

speechtext:
Apart from that remark, the minister's speech was apologetic and moderate. However, he did say that the municipalities administering the funds would realize their responsibility as a result of the reduction of the grant given them by the federal- government. Now the minister himself admitted that the municipalities are faced, not with a civic but with a national emergency, and when the emergency is national I think the national exchequer ought to come to the assistance of the municipalities much more generously than is the case at the present time. It can be said truthfully that there is no municipality in Canada that is either directly or indirectly responsible for unemployment among its people. If that is so, if our municipalities are in no way responsible for unemployment, why should a tremendous burden be imposed upon
Unemployment Relief

them-municipalities that are almost on the verge of bankruptcy. I do not know whether the federal grant to the municipalities is at present equivalent to twenty-five per cent of the amount of relief given. If the federal government were to give a fair proportion of relief to all municipalities, I do not think that a federal grant of fifty per cent would be at all too much. In fact, as pointed out by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland), in connection with the old age pensions the federal government grants seventy-five per cent. Yet if you want to argue the question of responsibility under the British North America Act, it might easily be argued that under that act the whole burden of old age pensions might be considered a provincial and local responsibility.
My purpose in rising at this time is to find out whether the government will not relax somewhat in their determination not to do anything on behalf of those nearly bankrupt municipalities and come to their assistance by giving a much larger contribution to the provincial authorities who in turn will thus be able to hand over a larger contribution to the municipalities and ease their burdens, so that they may be in a position to give a wider form of relief than is being given at the present time. I can assure the minister that the average municipality in this country is just as anxious to see that the funds of the dominion government are administered in an efficient manner as is the dominion government itself. In fact I have sat on several of those bodies that have been charged with the responsibility of handing out government relief, and when the relief is being administered representatives from the federal government have sat in on those bodies to see that the money is properly spent. There is no reason why under present circumstances the same representatives of the federal government should not sit in with these municipal and provincial bodies and see that the federal money is properly and wisely spent. I hope the Minister of Labour and those who are responsible for the Relief Act will at this time state that they are prepared to do something more than they have been doing so far to relieve the municipalities of an almost intolerable burden.

speechtext:
I want to lend some support to the contention put forward by the last speaker, the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I have not changed my opinion since first coming to the House of Commons. The intolerable position that the municipalities find themselves in at the

moment is in my judgment a problem that should receive the earnest and careful consideration of both federal and provincial governments. The municipalities are living under a taxation system that was devised to deal with their problems as we saw them fifty or sixty years ago. Old age pensions, mothers' ' allowances, education and the many other ramifications of social services, including road building as an hon. member suggests, that have been set in motion have in my opinion had too mudh of the responsibility in connection with them placed upon the shoulders of the municipalities when one considers the system of taxation that is in vogue in those municipalities. Then we come along to the depression which is national in its character, and I have always felt that in a national emergency a problem of this description should be within the orbit largely of the federal government, because it has many avenues of raising money of such a character that the burden does not fall most heavily upon the shoulders of those least able to bear it. We must remember this-and this is an important problem that must be faced in the next few years-that all these added charges have rested squarely upon real estate or, in other words, upon the shelter that is necessary for one living within the confines of an urban centre. I believe we have just about reached the saturation point, when one views the question from what I consider the best interests of our people, of the enormous charges that are being placed upon our real estate. We find in Ontario many municipalities going into default because of the burdens brought about by the charges underlying the relief programs of the respective governments.
There is another more important phase of the question that should be taken into consideration. I have always held the opinion and I have not changed it that if you give a man a sense of ownership of a 'home it has a stabilizing effect upon the country. These enormous taxation charges upon real estate are absolutely crippling the building and construction industry, and producing a nation of renters instead of owners. Freezing the building trades and checking the normal expansion of housing facilities, must lead inevitably to slum conditions. Taking a long view of the problem I do not think there is any argument about that.
I listened yesterday with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) when he said that Quebec was willing, provided the federal government would do likewise, to assume fifty per cent of the relief obligations of the municipalities in that

Unemployment Relief
province. I have before me a resolution that I wish to read into the record and which was passed by my own city council, referring to a similar proposition from the Ontario government. This resolution, which is under the signature of J. F. Berry, city clerk of Hamilton, Ontario, reads:
Whereas the premier of Ontario has publicly stated that the Ontario government would be willing to assume half the relief costs of the province providing the dominion government would pay the other half.
And whereas the burden of relief now being imposed' upon the municipalities has reached the point where it has become a very grievous burden and cannot much longer be borne.
Therefore be it resolved that this council place itself on record as approving of the offer made by the premier of Ontario and as urging the dominion government to accept the Ontario premier's offer at the earliest possible date; and that this council join with other municipalities in making representations to this end to the dominion government without delay; and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the dominion members of parliament for the city of Hamilton and county of Wentworth.
It might be said that the representatives of these municipalities are endeavouring to get out of what is probably their definite responsibility when one analyses the provisions of the British North America Act. That may be argued with some soundness, but I think hon. members and the provincial governments will agree that in the provision of relief for our people we have reached a stage where an entirely different policy should be set in motion from the viewpoint of raising revenue to provide for those who through no fault of their own find themselves at the moment unemployed. I remember stating in this house three years ago that the proper policy to be followed in regard to this important matter would have been to pay as we go, to carry the whole relief burden out of income, to place the responsibility where in my judgment it rightfully belongs, that is upon the shoulders of those who are best able to bear it. I believe the federal and provincial governments have the machinery to carry out such a policy, whereas on the other hand in the case of the municipalities the whole weight of the burden of debt rests upon land itself with practically only one avenue of taxation. I would like the government, before this bill finally becomes law, to give very serious consideration to the position that the home owner finds himself in, to the position that the municipality finds itself in, to the inevitable consequences of increasing taxes on land and to the question of lending its cooperation to those provincial governments that have suggested cooperative proposals, with the end in
view that the load be taken off the municipalities and that the basis of taxation for the provision of relief be placed upon those people who are better able to bear the burden and in avenues of taxation where the responsibility and the weight do not rest too heavily upon the lower paid salaried group in the dominion.	*

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it this bill is being passed in order to provide money for unemployment and farm relief. Coming as I do from a farming community I wish to protest most strenuously against unemployment and farm relief being linked together. In my opinion farm relief has nothing whatever to do with unemployment relief. I believe the people on the farms in western Canada, for example, have been busy for three hundred and sixty-five days in the past year; the people on the farms are not unemployed, and so far as I can see there is no good reason why they should be so classified and why funds should be provided for unemployment and farm relief in order to enable those people to subsist. To my way of thinking unemployment alone should be dealt with throughout the whole dominion; a sum of money should be divided up between the provinces, according to population if you like. For example, if you give the province of Saskatchewan S100,000 a month probably the province of Ontario should receive four times as much and the province of Quebec three times as much because of their greater population. But after this money has been divided among the different provinces in that way another problem arises in connection with the people who are working hard three hundred and sixty-five days in the year but who are getting nothing for their work. These people have suffered a catastrophe, and that situation should be dealt with entirely apart from any other situation, just as we would do if some calamity such as a flood or a fire occurred or, as has happened, if a drought should occur. Money should be granted these people in .order to help them out of their difficulties. As it is these people in western Canada have been classified as unemployed, whereas they have been employed all through the year though because of the unkindness of providence they have received nothing for their work.
I have heard hon. members say in this house that in the past year this government offered to take over and pay for farm relief in the dried out areas of western Canada. I want to say that I do not think the government of Saskatchewan or of any western

thought the man who paid for the music called the tune but apparently the government are paying the money while the pools are doing the work and taking all the credit or blame. I fail to see the reason for that situation. If the government are paying the money they are responsible. I think we should have some statement from this government, before they ask us to vote money for this sort of thing, in regard to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited and in regard to the money that has been granted them for speculation in the market, or to support the market or whatever they choose to call it. I repeat that to my way of thinking this is nothing more or less than a gamble. We have estimates with regard to wheat; I do not wish to go into that however, but wish simply to enter my protest with regard to granting money for this work without first having a report of what has been done in the past or where we stand ait the present time.

insufficient. I speak as one coming from the drought area of Manitoba, where in every year for the past while in order to carry on we have had to get grants from the federal treasury. While within the past few months I have not received a statement from the Minister of Finance, so far as the drought stricken area of Manitoba is concerned, I will say that that area has never to my knowledge requested money by way of advances from the federal government for these purposes which has been refused.
It is true that there are many who complain; it is true, also, that there are many who think the relief they are receiving is not sufficient, and there are those who are very happy to go around the country and state that the federal government is to blame. May I at this time mention something which in my own constituency I have had to point out thousands of times. The matter of administration of relief is entirely within the hands of the municipalities and the provinces. The amount of feed or the amount of relief of any kind which a man may receive is entirely in the discretion of the municipality in which he lives. They give him what relief they like; they have sole authority. The question of the money available is one which is arrived at through the municipality requesting the province for advances, and the province, in turn, requesting advances from the federal government. May I say that so far as the area with which I am connected is concerned, those advances have never been refused.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg states that the advances made by the federal government are equivalent only to 25 per cent of the total amount of relief. Again speaking only for my own area may I say, without making any mathematical calculation, that the advances are at least 75 per cent of the amount expended. This condition is due to the fact, first, that you have the direct advance made by the federal government, following which we have the federal government loaning one-third to the province, so that the province may pay its share of direct relief. Then, following that we have the federal government loaning to the province the remaining third, which in turn is handed on to the municipalities for purposes of covering the share payable by those municipalities.
In effect the federal government is, first, paying one-third outright, and then loaning the other two-thirds to the provinces for the purpose of paying the remainder of the relief moneys. The province, in turn, hands on one-half of the two-thirds to the municipality, and

in consequence the federal government assumes the responsibility for the whole 100 per cent. It pays one-third direct; it loans the other two-thirds,-and if you think the federal government will ever get that two-thirds back I am not in agreement with you.

works and pays 100 per cent. During the year 1931-32 there was a program of public works carried on for the cost of which the federal government paid 40, 50 or 60 per cent, the balance being paid by the provincial government or by the municipalities.
The hon. member for North Winnipeg points out that a number of municipalities are bankrupt. That is perfectly true. They must necessarily be bankrupt, due to the fact that no taxes are being received. The people who have had no crops cannot pay taxes; therefore the municipalities are bankrupt. May I point out to him however that the tax on the individual has not increased. It may be that the municipality has a greater debt, but it is also true that the taxation upon the individual farmer has not increased. The hon. member for North Winnipeg suggests that in this matter of loans the federal government might very well step in-

speechtext:
In the matter of administration, yes. May I say that at the present time there are employed in the area from which I come some three so-called administrators of the province of Manitoba. These three men go throughout the constituency administering relief and making decisions in regard to amounts of relief to be given. If the hon. member's suggestion were carried out the work would be exactly duplicated, because in each case the federal man would have to go with the provincial man and check and double check. But that is not possible. If it were it would double the cost of administration of relief. Therefore it could not properly be done. The question of the administration of relief should be placed where it properly belongs, namely, with the provinces and municipalities themselves.' To place it elsewhere would be to upset the whole system of government in this country.
The municipalities have their councils, their administrations which are familiar with the individual farms and localities. They are elected for that purpose. That is why it is necessary that they carry on administration, as they have done in the past. The question as to whether or not the municipality should be responsible for the administration of relief is well indicated by the fact that it has always been responsible for that administration when it has been necessary from year to year. As the relief has increased the jurisdiction of the municipality has not changed. The additional amount has merely

Unemployment Relief
increased the work the. municipality must do. The provinces, again, must have a responsibility in regard to administration, because the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces, and in each case get their authority from the provincial legislatures, Only the provincial legislatures have control over the municipalities; the federal government could not interfere with them because it has no jurisdiction. Further, it has no method of control.
The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) spoke particularly regarding relief for the drought area. If I understood him correctly I believe he suggested that we should divide relief by population. He suggested, if I heard him correctly, that we should divide it by population. No system I think could foe worse than that. In the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, from which he comes, how would he like to have the same amount of relief administered there as might be administered in one of the maritime provinces where relief was not necessary at all? Relief must necessarily be measured by need, and by nothing else. It must be measured by the needs of the people who are there.
The hon. member also spoke in regard to the classification of the farmer population as unemployed. I think I am correct in saying that that classification is not used. I have seen the documents coming into my municipalities, and they state on the bottom of each document, "For the drought area only." The advance of $135,000 had nothing to do with the drought area. The administration of relief in the drought area is an entirely separate matter, and if the hon. member for Willow Bunch will look up the administration in his own municipalities I have no doubt he will find that that is true.
The hon. member for Willow Bunch says that it is impossible to draw a dividing line to indicate where the drought areas are. But in the province of Manitoba that is precisely what has been done. He says it is impossible, but it has been done there for three years. Also, for his own province of Saskatchewan I have seen the map with the red marks on it indicating drought areas A, B and C, and the present government in the province of Saskatchewan has agreed to that map just as its predecessor did. In the province of Manitoba the lines marking the drought areas were drawn by the provincial government. I had the good fortune to come down with the provincial treasurer and in conference with him the drought areas in the 92582-122
province of Manitoba were defined by municipal boundaries. Drought area A is that in which for five years there has 'been no crop, and drought area B is the area which has not been afflicted so badly. Therefore the question of division is a very simple one which has been tackled and conquered in my hon. friend's own province, as well as in the province of Manitoba.
Finally the hon. member for Willow Bunch says that this government has been gambling in wheat. There was never a government in Canada which did so much for the wheat grower in Canada as this one has done in supporting the wheat market. I was much interested in seeing John I. McFarland before the banking and commerce committee and in hearing some of the hon. gentlemen opposite cross-examine him in regard to gambling in wheat. It was most amusing. I should rather see that again than go to any funny show I ever saw. My good friend Admiral Duff was one of those who cross-examined Mr. McFarland in regard to puts and calls, options and hedging. That is the difficulty with many people; they cannot distinguish between supporting the wheat market and gambling in wheat. It is true the process is technical. It is difficult to understand unless you have grown up with it at your table every morning. The wheat situation is difficult to understand unless you have lived in western Canada where every day on the street you must be prepared to talk about the price of wheat that day, what it opened at, what it was at twelve o'clock, what it closed at, and what the prospects are. So far as the question of supporting the wheat market is concerned I do not suppose that outside the hon. member for Willow Bunch there is any farmer in western Canada who would not say that the greatest help the wheat growers of western Canada have received from any government was the support given to the wheat market by Mr. McFarland in the way he did. Undouibtedly it is true that if that support had not been given, wheat would have gone down twenty or twenty-five or thirty cents a bushel more than it did. And let hon. gentlemen realize this, that where you have a man with only a few bushels on which he depends for his living, and when as a result of the government's support of the wheat market he receives from ten to twenty-five cents a bushel more than he otherwise would have done, that makes all * the difference between him being selfsupporting and becoming a charge on the Dominion of Canada. That is the difference,

Unemployment Relief

and that is the way it operates. On the other hand, if he is a big operator he is even worse off, because his losses will be greater.
It was interesting to note too that the hon. member for Willow Bunch pointed out in his remarks that Saskatchewan has not received proper treatment in the matter of relief. The actual relief which has been advanced to Saskatchewan is some $20,740,000, and loans have been granted amounting to $38,000,000, which gives us a grand total advanced to Saskatchewan, from which the hon. member comes, of $58,743,000. Those are the advances that have been made by this government since 1930. If you will look at it carefully that seems to be a very large sum of money. But in addition to that, there is the amount which was given to the province of Saskatchewan under the wheat bonus. Saskatchewan grows more wheat than any other province or any other area of similar size probably in the world, and on that account Saskatchewan received a larger share of the bonus. That is important to consider in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Willow Bunch, who if I remember correctly voted against that bill, which makes it all the worse.
The question of relief, and the question of federal government assistance in the matter of relief, is one which most of the municipalities and most of the provinces and a large number of individuals would like to shoulder upon this dominion government, but may I point this out to the house and the country, that every individual, every municipality, every province and every dominion has its limit of credit beyond which it cannot go, and if we are to continue to play Santa Claus to the municipalities and the provinces, not based on the question of need, then sooner or later we are going to face in this country a situation similar to that with which other countries are now faced. Canada has perhaps the unique record of having paid all its debt according to the letter of the contract, with the result that we have been able to borrow money at as low a rate as two per cent, resulting largely from that splendid record. Some people point to Great Britain as having done well in regard to its contracts. May I point out that Canada has done much better. Great Britain herself has not honoured all her debts to foreign countries in the way that Canada has, and that is one reason why the credit of this country stands so high. The dominion government, due to the fact that the municipalities are spread from one end of this country to the other, is not in the same position to defend itself as the municipalities and the provinces, and I am kept
TMr. Willis.]
busy going around the country refuting statements that the dominion government has not done this or won't do that, and in ninety-nine per cent of these cases the charge is quite unfounded. The dominion government itself is partly to blame for that because it has been too silent on these matters. It should come out openly and blazon forth what it has done and is doing rather than stand back and receive the criticism which comes upon the individual member who must go around and defend the position of the government.
The advances made by the federal government to Manitoba have been satisfactory, and its advances for the drought area in the province from which I come have been satisfactory. It is not dealing with the administration of relief, and I do not think it should. While I myself have complained in regard to certain small matters of relief by the federal government, I think that by and large the handling of the relief situation in the drought areas on behalf of this government has been nothing less than excellent.
Mr. VALLAN'CE: Mr. Chairman, when the house met at three o'clock I had no intention of taking part in a discussion on this bill but I have been forced into it. I had hoped that a discussion on wheat would not take place at this time. There is on the order paper a resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) which reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to establish a board to be known as the Canadian grain board-
When that board is established the functions now performed by Mr. John I. McFarland will have to be done away with. I should like to know whether the government is in a position to give to the house and to the country a full statement of the operations of Mr. McFarland in the wheat market. The resolution to which I have referred may be only a red herring drawn across the trail in an effort to prevent a discussion of this very important question, but whether or not that is so I think the house and the country should have a statement of these operations. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) referred to the tactics or antics of some hon. members on this side of the house in the banking and commerce committee when John I. McFarland was before that body. Ever since this gentleman started his operations I have stood out boldly in support of the contentions of the government. I did not believe then that it was in the interests of the grower that the position of Mr. McFarland in the wheat market should be divulged and I maintained

Unemployment Relief
that position, both in the committee and in the house. However, I think the time has now come when this should be done. We are nearing a general election and I do not think this house should be asked to pass this bill before it receives a statement either by the Prime Minister or the minister now piloting this bill through the house.
I say quite frankly but kindly that I do not think the gentlemen sitting before the minister or the minister are in a position to give this statement. John I. McFarland should be sitting in front of the minister. There are only two men in this country who can give satisfaction in this matter, John I. McFarland and the Prime Minister. It is regrettable that the Prime Minister is not in his place and it seems impossible to have Mr. McFarland occupy a seat in front of the minister. I was hoping that when we reached the resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister we would have the assurance of the government that the bill which would be based upon it would be sent either to the agriculture committee or to a special committee. That would enable all hon. members, all growers and all marketers to appear before the committee to give evidence. In my opinion the government would be well advised to give us some assurance that this resolution will actually be brought before the house. If the resolution is not	to be proceeded with, then the
government should immediately make known their position in the wheat market. I believe the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) will admit that I am reasonable in asking him whether he can give us an assurance that this resolution will be dealt with before the house prorogues.
I realize that the bill passed last year expires on the last day of this month and, therefore, this bill must be passed before that time in order to provide funds for Mr. McFarland to operate.	When I saw the
nature of the resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister I did not expect any discussion of this matter under the present bill. I should like the minister to state if it is the intention of the government to give us the information for which we are asking. Up until the present I did not think it was in the interests of the grower-he is the individual in whom I am interested- to make known the position of the government. As the hon. member for Souris has said I think the government should feel that they should make a statement to the country.
Can the minister tell us how much has been spent for unemployment relief and how much for farm relief? It was rather annoying to hear the hon. member for Souris say that the government did not expect that much of this money would be paid back. I have heard the Prime Minister say the same thing.	,

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, even
though I am a member from one of the larger municipalities in Ontario, one which is probably more interested in this particular bill than other municipalities, I would not have spoken had it not been for the fact that economic liberalism has failed to give us any constructive ideas or offer a policy to take our people off the dole and restore Canada to the Canada of Sir John A. Macdonald's day. At that time Canada was a country of property owners, both large and small; it was not divided as now into a country of those who have and those who have not. At that time the entire means of production of the country was not in the hands of five or six people. I want to pay tribute to the government for what they have done since the great disaster which occurred in 1930. If this parliament had followed the example of the British parliament we would have had a united legislature on social matters like this, which would have acted to try to keep our people from relief. We have a war in Canada to-day against unemployment and famine, great masses of the population being on relief. Surely no one will deny that this is as dangerous as any enemy in warfare. When an enemy is at our gates we mobilize our whole military organization and repel the
Unemployment Reliej

invader; we are united; we present a united front to the enemy. But when we have what is as great a menace to the country, hundreds of thousands of the population on the verge of starvation or in poorhouses through unemployment, we are divided, playing politics, the polities of the ins and outs, as we have witnessed this afternoon. I am . surprised especially at my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell), who is more or less a sportsman. I spoke in his ridihg for the late Colonel Rennie. The constituency of East Hamilton is a large industrial one and this government has done a good deal for the people there. I am therefore surprised that my hon. friend should have voted against the second reading of the bill, because industrial society in the country was entirely built up by the Conservative party's policy of protection from 1878 down. What is that policy? It is a protection policy which if brought up to date will remove the working population from the dole, the pension and all that sort of thing. But what have my hon. friends opposite done, : those of the official opposition and those to the left of them? Some voted for the second reading and others did net. I had expected that the hon. member for East Hamilton would vote for it, because if there is a riding that owes something to the present government for what it has done in the way of relief it is that riding.
I congratulate the minister on what he has done in connection with relief and unemployment. I know no man who has shouldered a greater responsibility than he has taken on in the last five years, with the exception of our great leader who is not with us to-day, a martyr to overwork. As a former president of the Union of Canadian Municipalities, I can say that the municipalities are having a hard struggle. The minister is doing the best he can to cope with a very difficult situation and I congratulate him. He is a very able minister as well as an able lawyer, and more than that he is a man with a warm human heart. In the past four years he has done a good deal for relief in this country. I remember sitting in this house and hearing the former Prime Minister make statements declining aid to the municipalities with regard to relief which disappointed me at the time. I do not see him here to-day. I was glad to see that he received yesterday such a tribute from his supporters, and it is better for a man to have such tributes paid him when he is living. He is a man who has given a great deal of study to these particular social matters, but
	,
I regret that when he was head of the government from 1921 to 1930 he did nothing to deal with the situation. I constantly brought this matter to the attention of parliament. The other day I read various resolutions, which I will not read again, all bearing on this subject, but the right hon. gentleman said that he would not give a five cent piece to the people of Ontario, and that included the riding of East Hamilton. I put certain questions to his Minister of Labour, Mr. Heenan, as late as February 25, 1929. I asked him questions in regard to relief, not only on behalf of the municipality I represented but as one of the former officers of the union to which I have already referred. In 1929 I asked this question:
1.	Has the government any plans for providing employment for the great body of the unemployed?	_
2.	If so, what are they and what action will be taken, and when?
Mr. Heenan:
1.	The question of unemployment is one for the provincial governments.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
On March 5, 1930, after deputations had been here from the provinces and the municipalities, following two years of relief, and having made a request for assistance, this was the question I asked:
1.	Has the government any plans for providing useful employment for the great body of the unemployed?
2.	If so, what relief will be afforded?
3.	Will the government accept the offer of the province of Ontario to provide one-third of the cost of certain forms of relief in connection with the federal and municipal authority; if not, why not?
What happened then? The leader of the government of that day rose in his place and objected to the question; a page of Hansard was taken up with an effort to have my question ruled out of order. There was in South Toronto at one or two missions and in other places a line-up of the unemployed begging for meals, but we were told that that unemployment was a matter for the provinces and the municipalities to deal with. Even Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier never had to face the conditions with which this government has had to contend since 1930. In 1928 I brought the matter to the attention of the house and asked the government to appoint a commission similar to the one that had been appointed in the United States, under the chairmanship of Senator Couzens, who was mayor of Detroit. This committee sat many months at Washington and they summoned to Washington some of the greatest men in engineering, agriculture and the banking system. They studied the question of

Unemployment Reliej
seasonal unemployment, casual unemployment and technological unemployment growing out of the inroads of science and the machine. When it was proposed in this house that we should have a commission of that kind, what did the government of that day do? They not only refused to accede to the request, but Mr. Heenan actually informed me that there was no unemployment on the index findings, and if any it was a matter for the municipalities. Mr. Willard, president of the Baltimore & Ohio Railway, at that time made this statement before the Senate committee at Washington:
It is a dangerous thing to have a large number of unemployed men and women

dangerous to society as a whole-dangerous to the individuals who constitute society. When men who are willing and able to work and want to work are unable to obtain work, we need not be surprised if they steal before they starve. Certainly I do not approve of stealing, but if I had to make the choice between stealing and starving, I would surely not choose to starve- and in that respect I do not think I am much unlike the average individual.
The commission in the United States took evidence from all sources, the railways and other organizations, the municipalities, boards of trade and chambers of commerce, for the purpose of evolving a policy, three years before the depression started.
I wish now to say a word or two with regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) in connection with the municipalities. The municipalities have only a limited number of ways of raising revenue, though they render to the federal government many invaluable municipal services in connection with police protection, fire protection and so on. In the case of Ottawa they get a subvention, and the state legislatures of the United States also give the capital cities a subvention. The same is true in Australia. Yet in the industrial centres large numbers of people are out of work, and a considerable proportion of them who own their own homes cannot pay their taxes. The municipalities are finding it very difficult to balance their budgets. I plead with the government now as I have pleaded with them on many occasions to come to the support of the municipalities. The government have many ways of raising revenue directly and indirectly which the municipalities do not have, and I plead with the government of the day to do something along those lines. The government that preceded this one declined to do anything for the municipalities, but the present government decided to give one-third in cooperation with the provincial and municipal authorities.
Hon. gentlemen in the extreme left comer think they are the only labour party in this house. I represent a labour constituency. With my friend the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Spence) and others in the city council I helped to put through an eight hour day, pensions and many other things. Some of this was done in 1909, twenty-six years ago. Hon. gentlemen who sit in the extreme left corner do not constitute the only labour party in the house. The Conservative party in this chamber has done more for labour than has any other party. There is for instance the Workman's Compensation Act, the national policy and public ownership. This party has built up industrial society by its policy of protection, of giving our own work to our own workmen, of maintaining our own markets for our own products. This has been a consistent policy of the Conservative party; it has been applied consistently from 1878 down to the present day to ninety-eight per cent of the people. Where would the agricultural workers who constitute fifty per cent of the population be to-day if we had free trade or semi-free trade as preached on the prairies by some hon. gentlemen in the official opposition and some in the extreme left corner? In those days when Mr. Crerar was in the house, we heard about the plight of the poor grain growers and we heard charges about the elevator combines, and middlemen, grain exchanges, and the transportation combines. The poor grain grower had more to fear from these big interests west of the great lakes than they had from the manufacturers east of the great lakes through the middlemen, the elevator combines, the transportation combines and the grain exchanges. Where was official liberalism at that time? It was lined up with the free traders, the semi-free traders and some of the Progressives who proclaimed that the grain-growing industry was a north south industry and not an east and west industry to the markets of the world. There should be some honour among politicians as among sportsmen, but there does not seem to be as much. You can please nobody; you get no credit for anything. The government receives no credit for what it has done, but I admit that is only human nature. However, if ever there were a government that honestly endeavoured to do something for the working people of this country in this emergency, it is the one that now sits on this side of the house.
We are asked by the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who is very fond of dealing with the constitution if our legislation war
The Royal Assent

constitutional. What did the government do in the fall of 1930? They were faced with the British North America Act, that comedy of errors; they could do very little or nothing, but they very fortunately found three or four words "peace, order and good government." It was very fortunate for the working people and for the municipalities that those words were found by a very able lawyer, the Prime Minister, and another able lawyer [DOT] with him, the Minister of Labour. Many municipalities will agree that they would have been bankrupt had it not been for the clause "peace, order and good government" and the blank cheque. The blank cheque is really not a blank cheque at all. Hon. gentlemen opposite refused to give a five-cent piece for relief. I have before me some fifteen or sixteen pages taken from Hansard of those years, but I shall not read them here. Hon. members can read those statements in Hansard of the questions and answers. Where would the municipalities be; where under those conditions would be the city of Hamilton from which the hon. member for East Hamilton comes? They would not have had one cent for industry or relief in that city had it not been for the money they got through the present Minister of Labour carrying out the policy of this party. At that time it was contended in the house by the ex-Minister of Labour that I was always talking about unemployment; I was told on one occasion that I was preaching blue ruin by persisting in bringing up the question. One hon. gentleman, I think it was Sir Henry Drayton, said that I had need to. I was one of the heads of a municipality for many years and I know a municipality, irrespective of politics, must appreciate what this government has done. As a follower of municipal institutions in this country, I believe that was only a start in the right direction. The government should go over the books and see whether something cannot be done further for our struggling municipalities.
In this particular case I was hoping that we would hear some constructive ideas about handling this problem of unemployment from economic liberalism and from hon. gentlemen in the extreme left corner. I appeal to' the opposition and through them to the provinces, to the churches and boards of trade to help the government pull the country out of the mire in regard to this particular problem of relief. Let us not depend upon the British North America Act, the constitution; the people cannot buy bread by depending on the British North America Act; the butchers and grocers will not give them food because of it.

The welfare of man in such days of universal want as these transcends the future of any political party, and it is too bad all parties do not unite on common ground to solve our problems free of partisanship. This course has been followed in England. On a social measure private members there were allowed hv the government the other day to give their views freely and they were invited to do so. One or two of the ministers got up in the British house and opposed the government oill. The whips were called off and the members were allowed to express themselves freely. Here we are to-day, two hundred and forty-five members sitting in a committee presided over by our very popular deputy speaker, and I say that we as a committee should forego politics and do as they did in England regarding this problem-get down to brass tacks and see what should be done. Every time I hear the opposition talk, they plead the constitution; dissertations on the British North America Act are made by the ex-Minister of Justice and others.

speechtext:
May I say that I had not concluded my observations. Hon. members opposite have been very fond of quoting the British North America Act, but they have not suggested any constructive policy whereby our people could be taken off the dole and put back to work. They put me in mind of Mr. Boythorn in Bleak House, and the canary which he fondled on his finger all the time he was shouting his most lurid denunciations. Hon. members opposite are content to sit back and talk about the constitution all the time at a time when people are starving and in a position where some have to go to the poor house. After all is said and done, the duty of the hour is to get the people off the dole and back to work. The reconstruction of our country and a higher standard of living is the object before the party on this side of the house. Industry in Canada, in short, must re-adapt itself to the home market, and this is a most complicated process. It cannot be done by individual effort
We know that in England to-day they are developing their land to the point where they will not have to depend on a foreign food supply. W e know that in this country national trade is decreasing, and it would seem that a revival of industry could come only from a greater consumption in the home market. We must push the country forward by planning for a higher economic and social standard, and in this effort we want a united country and the support of every part of it. This is a national work and must have the support of all people. The situation calls for national sacrifices instead of parliamentary repartee and playing the game of the ins and the outs. Church, state, the press and individuals will have to unite and no class or function should be left out. Every person should be in it.
I should like to say a word or two as to what should be done to bring our men off the dole, and place them in a position whereby they may have homes. A short time ago in his budget message the President of the United States said that their people would have to be taken off the dole. He said the policy followed was uneconomic and foreign to their constitution. I believe in this country we could do very much by way of reconstruction. We could do such work as Italy is now doing -reforestation, river improvements, drainage, irrigation, sewers, roads, work on river banks, provision for domestic water supply, harbour work, schools, municipal services, water supply for farmers, house building and work of other kinds. A similar program of work could be adapted to this country and to our circumstances on a third basis, with municipal and provincial authority on a large construction policy, which would be better than the dole.
The dole is only temporary; it is not a final remedy. People want work and that is the only lasting cure. Franchises from the people giving charters to corporations involving the assumption by such corporations of corresponding debts and obligations. These corporations owe a debt to their creator, the public. They should repay this debt to the public from whom they have derived their powers. If they fail in their duty, the community which created them would be justified in stepping in and exercising some control over their future actions.
The Conservative party has always been constructive. It has to its credit reform legislation such as the eight hour day bill and legislation for a minimum wage. This party is equipped by position and temperament to bring better order into Canadian life and industry, and to check the abuses which affect the consumer and the labourer. We should remove some of the unethical business practices, and bring protection up to date, eliminate the abuses to protect consumer and labour, and prevent further burdens and artificial barriers being placed on business. The main problem to be solved in Canada is unemployment. That is the main problem because no scheme of pensions and no scheme of unemployment insurance is a substitute for work and wages and the desire of people to work. Employment is the only real agency by which the nation's wealth can be distributed. Without consumption, production is a mere waste, and work and wages for all is the main agency of distribution. This party was the founder of protection, and it should dedicate itself to solving this problem of distributism and of getting people off the dole and back to work
Unemployment Relief

Agriculture has always been traditionally associated with the Conservative party. As a party we stand for the further development and preservation of the home market for agriculture. Our own markets for our own products, and our own work for our own workmen is our policy. Agriculture is the oldest of our industries from the point of view of employment. It has been content to choose order instead of anarchy, and industry can be made amenable to similar treatment.
The solution of our economic problems calls for large sacrifices. The war made a great difference. The vast amount of voluntary work done and the great outburst of patriotism in times of danger are sure signs in Canada of a national spirit which will help the government to cope with the present dangers. Are we as a people, equal to our problems? For thirty years we have neglected to notice the inroads upon unemployment of science and the machine. A manufacturer puts in a machine for the specific purpose of lowering costs and to enable him to undercut his competitors at home and aboard. The item which is reduced by the machine is labour alone. That is the very purpose of the machine, to put people out of work, and it has succeeded admirably in its purpose. The machine has meant a large increase of female employment and a decrease of male employment. Formerly it was assumed that the labour displayed by the machine would be absorbed in other forms of work, but that is an absurd position for industry to be in because the welfare of man is the first duty of the government and of civilization. I belieye. that the Conservative party and the opposition should unite to solve the problem of distributism.
The Liberal party of this country to-day represents the last stand of economic liberalism in Canada. It relies on these social measures being declared unconstitutional. It is the party that for nine years had a chance to do something along these lines, but only dillydallied. It is the same party which in England opposed the factory acts and free schools, and the liberation of the trade unions. To-day it concentrates its attention in Canada on the tariff and on wider markets, when wider markets are not available. The Liberal party in Canada is an advocate of social reform, pensions, doles, social insurance-all these are in its platform for the higher life, but they refuse to give to this house a plan or platform to grapple with the cause and effects of the social revolution and with those economic factors which deprive men of the bread of their own production and the fruits of their

own toil. I believe' that free trade and the error of the Liberal party's policies have been to the detriment of agriculture and of industry in Canada. Many children are in factories to-day who should be in school, and most of the young offenders who come before our courts are underprivileged children many of them from poverty stricken homes, who from birth have never had a proper chance.
I believe we should give some credit to the gentlemen who sit in the far corner of the house because in 1928, 1929 and 1930 they did bring to the attention of the government the question of unemployment and they supported a policy of direct relief. But some of them are not consistent and do not vote with the government of the day. I would ask them to remember that the government has done the best it could, faced with that comedy of errors called the British North America Act, a relic of the ox-cart days. Faced with that act I do not see what further they could have done. We are told that we have to suffer all these social evils because of the British North America Act, because certain wise men away back in 1867, whose vision was poor and shortsighted, unloaded the provincial system on us as opposed to the federal system as they have it in England and the United States. A lot of the things we have to-day were unheard of in 1867. There were no joint stock companies in 1867, no telephones, no power development, no NRA., no air lines, no radios, no old age pensions, no social insurance, no eight hour day; nor had many of the great discoveries been made in science, physics and biology, with which we are familiar to-day. Are we to assume that the fathers who lived in the past have left us adequate machinery to deal with the problems that these new discoveries have brought us? As I said the other day, one of the most important things we must do before we can solve any of these problems in a practical way is to have constitutional and parliamentary reform in this country. The greatest problem they have in England to-day is constitutional and parliamentary reform, and they cannot make social progress without it. The authors of the British North America Act did not play bridge or squash or badminton, but they left us this relic, the British North America Act, and as a result the unemployed have to suffer and we can solve no economic or social question. It would be far better for us to face the fact that that act is in need of reform. Unemployment and relief have now reached their peak, and the tide is receding very rapidly. I believe that before

Unemployment Relief
spring is over, with a housing and reconstruction policy, the peak of relief will have been passed, and I hope that men will be getting back to work.

speechtext:
May I say to my
hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Church) that when he did not rise after we suspended our sitting for royal assent, I assumed he had finished his speech. What I began to say was that the unsatisfactory nature of an omnibus measure of this kind has been very clearly illustrated b/ the kind of debate, if it may be so dignified, which has taken place upon it. My colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) began by speaking of unemployment relief, stressing particularly the plight of the industrial worker and the difficulties that confront the municipalities. Next we had two hon. members referring to the troubles in the dried out areas, this having nothing whatever to do with city problems. The next speaker referred to the wheat arrangement, thus introducing a new topic. In this connection I think we might very easily refer to the loans to the Canadian Pacific Railway which were made several years ago under a measure of this kind. We could refer also to the writing up of the assets of the insurance companies, and we could make mention of the peace, order and good government provisions. Reference might also be made to the financial position of the various provinces. In these circumstances I submit it becomes almost impossible to focus attention upon any one measure and to secure the opinion of the house in that regard. The hon. member for East Toronto has expressed himself as being disappointed with the labour members not voting in favour of the measure. I did not speak on the second reading of the bill, but I think I can say that we voted against the motion for second reading for three reasons. First of all, we voted against the motion because of the inadequacy of the measure to meet the actual needs of the people. No indication is given that there is to be adequate relief, and no mention is made of what the relief works, if any are contemplated, are to be. Next, the bill provides for the exercise by the government of very wide powers, much wider than should be granted by a measure of this kind. These questions have been threshed out in the discussion of similar measures during the past two or three years and I do not intend to repeat the arguments then advanced. Still further, we voted against this motion as a protest against the lack of assumption by the
government of anything like responsibility for the national emergency which now confronts the country.
The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) stated that the administration of relief should be placed where it belongs, with the municipalities and provinces. As I understood him, he implied that the responsibilities for relief lay essentially with the municipalities and the provinces, and that certainly is implied by the preamble of the bill now before us. Under these circumstances I should like to read once more what has been read into the record again and again. I would not do this were it not for the fact that the hon. member for Souris has sought to condone the inaction of the government. I should like to quote from a speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in Calgary on June 12, 1930, as follows:
But this is a new country, and there is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if a government does its duty.
Is that true or is it not true? If it was true when the Prime Minister spoke in Calgary in 1930, surely it is true in 1935. The Prime Minister was then asking to be entrusted with authority to carry on the affairs of the country, and he said:
I say to you, my fellow citizens, my fellow Canadians, speaking to the larger audience, I am convinced this problem has now ceased to be local and provincial and has become national in its importance.
I contend that if that were true in 1930 it is just as true in 1935, and perhaps more so. The Prime Minister was then seeking a mandate from the people. He said:
I propose that parliament shall formulate a definite plan for permanent relief, and that parliament, as representing the people, shall deal with this national problem and provide amelioration for the condition in order that next winter the Canadian people may not be facing the crisis that is upon us without having a remedy at hand.
After five years in public office he brings forward a measure of this kind, a measure which is inadequate and which we should not be asked to support. In voting as I did, I did not repudiate the action of the dominion government in offering relief. If that were the question before us I would hold up both hands for the motion. What I tried to do with my vote was to protest-I think this is true also of my colleagues-against the inadequate manner in which the government is providing for the needs of the unemployed, and the fact that after five years they have gone back on the solemn pledges made to the electorate in 1930. It is only
Unemployment Relief

within the last few months that the Prime Minister in his radio speeches repudiated in the very strongest language the idea of the dole. I agree with the hon. member for East Toronto that we should endeavour to place all our people in constructive work of some kind. That has not been done, and the minister sits silent when we speak of the necessity of a further extension of public works. We cannot get any action from the government, and il contend that we were justified in voting against the motion as a protest against the lack of a policy on the part of the government.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer; it comes under the heading of peace, order and good government. A couple of nights ago we were discussing the estimates of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Stirling). In giving a reason for the maintenance of an army in this country, the minister said:
In addition it fulfils another day, that the force should be distributed throughout Canada in the military districts in such a way that if called upon by the provincial governments in time of stress and strain, through civil disturbances within their own boundaries, they can render such assistance as may be necessary to support the police forces of the country.
We spend something like $20,000,000 upon the military forces of this country and the mounted police, which is a semi-military force. My contention is that if a fraction of this sum were spent upon setting in motion certain constructive forces which would take care of the unemployed we would be much further advanced. Under peace, order and good government we are giving to the government the power to protect and maintain the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof. I say again that if the unemployed were absorbed into industry, that if a greater purchasing power were given to the people, it would provide the best means of maintaining and protecting the financial position of the dominion and the provinces. It seems to some of us that the government is more solicitous in protecting the credit of the country than it is in protecting the welfare of the people. Only the other day I had a letter from a friend living in the constituency of Souris. He referred to a district which I knew very intimately thirty or forty years ago. He spoke of the run-down condition of the houses, the outbuildings, the machinery and the interior of the homes, he spoke of the despair and the demoralization of people who a few years ago were prosperous farmers; and his concluding sentence, if I remember rightly, 
was, "and the young people have nearly all moved away." Now how can we have a prosperous country with conditions of that kind? Someone might very well say that drought is a dispensation of Providence, and that we cannot be held responsible for the climatic changes in the drought area. That is true, but we are responsible for the morale of the people, to see that it is maintained; and the morale of the people can be maintained only as they are given some hope for the future. But so far we have had no clear-cut plan which indicates that the people in these vast areas may have any immediate hope.
I submit that of much greater importance than providing for military and police protection or providing for the maintenance of the credit of this country is provision for the people to live decently. To-day we are in practice trying so to arrange matters that no one will starve. There are occasional instances of actual starvation, and there are more instances of suicide caused by anxiety. But on the whole we are trying to see to it that no one actually starves. But we are keeping tens of thousands of our people on the bare subsistence line and allowing them this subsistence only at the expense of what we have considered a part of their manhood and) womanhood'-their self-respect. We degrade them by giving them charity. I would ask why it could not be arranged that every unemployed citizen should have a pension as a matter of right, not of charity but as a matter of right. In recent times we have been rather inclined to laugh at the Townsend plan in the United States, where an individual has come out and urged that a very large pension should- be paid to everyone over the age of sixty. Probably Doctor Townsend has altogether overdone his proposals along this line, but the fact that he has such a large following is the result not merely of a demagogic appeal but of the realization by the people that the ordinary citizen has certain rights to a decent living.
I am not advocating what has come to be known as the " national dividend " as a part of the social oredit scheme, as put forward by Major Douglas. I confess that I do not understand the theories of Major Douglas, but I do say that that phase of it contains a real measure of truth, and because it does it is appealing to tens of thousands of people. Why should the people who have helped to build up this country and are now thrown out of work through no fault of their own not obtain a reasonable pension, if you like to call it that, as a matter of right? Even

Unemployment Relief
this afternoon I heard someone refer in rather disparaging terms to the unemployed as if they belonged to an inferior class. I protest against that way of viewing unemployment; I protest against our thinking that anything given in the way of unemployment relief is a form of charity. It should not be so regarded. I quite admit that in the old days under normal conditions when a man was out of work it was usually through some fault of his own; he was shiftless or a drunkard or something of that kind, and naturally the municipality was required to take care of him. But that is not the situation to-day with regard to the great majority of those who are unemployed, and for that reason the burden should not be loaded on to the municipalities. It is not a local matter. The municipalities have had nothing to say with regard to the vast immigration to this country. They have had nothing to say with regard to trade conditions in this country, with regard to the war and its consequences, with regard to the financial arrangements of the country. The dominion government is responsible for these general policies, and that being so I take it that the dominion government should assume responsibility for the effects of these policies. It is not fair now to load the responsibility on the provinces or the municipalities.
It may be thought that in advocating something in the form of a general pension I am simply making an appeal to the gallery. I hope that those who know me will not think so; I hope they will not think, either, that I am guilty of a kind of impossible idealism. Not at all. I say that we are actually giving food, clothing and shelter and in some instances medical assistance, besides light, heat, and requirements of that kind, to large numbers of these people, but we are giving this assistance grudgingly in the form of charity, and that policy is having the effect of creating all sorts of friction between the municipality and the province and the dominion and at the same time demoralizing the people who receive the assistance.
Someone may claim that those receiving relief ought to have contributed to some unemployment pension scheme. Well, we have had no such scheme to which they could have contributed and you cannot initiate such a scheme that will at once meet the existing situation. On the other hand the great majority of those people who are now unemployed and in need of relief have contributed in the past to the welfare of the country, working in our factories, our shops
and offices, in our railways and other constructive work. These are the people who are unemployed to-day. Why should we load the whole burden of the depression upon this one group of people? I do not think that anyone in Canada has a right to even a comfortable income so long as these people are on the dole, and much less do I think that any man has a right to enjoy a large income so long as large numbers of our people can subsist only by asking for charity. This question goes deep; it is fundamental in our national life. Is the whole machinery of Canadian government being maintained in order to maintain the status quo, in order that we may preserve a condition under which a few are deriving great benefits while equally worthy Canadians are being not only thrown out of work but thrown upon charity? I submit that after five years in office the government should be held responsible for making provision for the situation which confronts us.
The hon. member for East Toronto rather deprecated the fact that measures of this kind immediately become party measures. We all feel sorry that this is so, and in the newspapers in the last few weeks there has been a good deal of talk of a national government as a way out. Personally I am strongly opposed to a national government such as is contemplated by those who advocate it.
