speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are now considering bill 41 for the relief of unemployed throughout the country. The preamble of this bill is as follows:
Whereas the provinces may require further assistance in carrying out necessary relief measures and in meeting financial conditions
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
as the same may arise; and whereas in such event it is in the national interest that parliament should support and supplement the relief measures of the provinces and grant them financial assistance in such manner and to such extent as the governor in council may deem expedient.	.
Do you not think, Mr. Chairman, that we should take this opportunity to avail ourselves of the benefits offered by this bill, in order to support an institution that is truly national by its nature: I am referring to the great French university, of this beautiful university which we have in this country, the University of Montreal.
Some years ago, full of confidence in the future of our race and of our province, a few courageous men decided to enrich our metropolis with as perfect a . university as could be justified by the place that we occupy in the world, as the second largest French city.
It was a grand undertaking, but it was also a plan that sprang from the purest patriotism, from the legitimate pride of our race and from our desire to give the intellectual elite of our province the means of improving their university training and teaching, in order bo produce a greater number of highly qualified men, so that the people of our race may take their rightful place in the intellectual and economic spheres, and also to rouse dormant talents, to bring them to light and make them contribute to a larger extent to the intellectual and material progress of Canada.
Seven million dollars have been spent on that building and since three years all work has been stopped for lack of funds; seven millions engulfed in that undertaking; seven millions which remain unproductive. The future of our race is linked with the development of our higher studies. If we suffer from a marked inferiority wherever education counts, in the industrial field as well as in the technical departments of the Dominion or even provincial government, it is because we always lacked the financial means to properly develop our higher studies and produce capable men which among our people are ever present in a latent state.
I do not wish to establish as a principle that only educated men may succeed in the material sphere. That would mean that all our business men and all those who acquired wealth owe their success to their higher education. No, that is not true, but it is a fact that all those who succeeded owe it mostly to their ability in surrounding themselves with educated and competent men whose efforts they directed for their own benefit. Well, our

Unemployment Relief
English speaking fellow citizens had among their own, people a larger number of competent men whose services they utilized to build up their fortune; and we unfortunately realize that among our own people, those who succeeded owe it to their association with another race than their own, not because we are less intelligent, but because we are not as well prepared for the acquisition of wealth.
The distinguished rector of Laval University of Quebec, Mgr. Camille Roy, sounded the alarm in his last lecture before the Canadian Club in Quebec. He attributed our inferiority in industry and the civil service to the insufficient development of our higher education, due to a lack of funds among our universities. When such a distinguished man, who has devoted all his life to education and who is perhaps the highest authority among our educational leaders, points out so clearly what our educational system lacks; when he mentions what is probably the greatest cause of our inferiority in this Dominion, can we possibly fold our arms and witness the falling off of our educational system without raising our voice?
We are a race of individualists, ordinarily incapable of voluntarily sacrificing ourselves to allow others to build with our money, although, in times of crisis, we are ready to sacrifice ourselves enthusiastically for the common salvation. So great is our respect for civil and religious authority, so strong is our belief in the strength and power of the church and of the state that we never seriously entertain the idea that they may really need our help. We are accustomed to leave our educational problem to our clergy and our religious institutions with never a thought of helping them. And our clergy perform each year the miracle of providing us with an education as nearly perfect as possible with a budget five times smaller than that of the English schools and universities.
Compare, for instance, the resources of our university with those of McGill. McGill university, with endowments and investments amounting to $18,566,463 and grounds, buildings and equipment valued at $12,826,845, has total assets of $31,393,308 and enjoyed, in 1931, a revenue of $2,480,914. For the same year, the University of Montreal owned in endowments and investments the sum of $221,366, compared with McGill's 18 millions, and grounds and buildings valued at $7,898,010, making total assets of $8,119,376, against McGill's 31 millions. Our university's revenue amounted to $253,644, against McGills' two and a half millions. I shall spare you further
statistics for the moment, but these figures alone show the miracle which our university accomplishes each year in giving us so complete an education with such limited resources. There is one thing, howetver, that makes us hope to possess some day a university as complete as McGill. Our university buildings are valued at 8 millions, compared with McGill's 12 millions. About three million dollars more are required to complete the work undertaken, so that when these three millions have been spent We will have a university fully as well equipped as McGill.
The question now arises of where to get these three millions. In the face of the present world-disrupting crisis, we do not know what to do. It is clear that, had the prosperity of 1927 continued, we would have no university problem; the public would have subscribed all the money required.: But prosperity is no longer with us. Why? To a certain extent, we do not know. However, the condition exists and we have to fight it. But it is useless to recriminate and to attribute the responsibility to others, as each one is probably responsible to some extent for the present state of affairs. The crisis seems to be largely due to a lack of general orientation. Every man and every government knows something about it, but the policy followed with the greatest conviction by every one is to do nothing. Feeling ourselves isolated and not knowing which way to turn, we have so to speak organized a strike of our resources and capital.
To put an end to this intolerable situation, there is need of a practical policy founded on order, logic and method. What solution have we so far found for this problem? Direct relief. It is generally admitted that the direct relief system is demoralizing our population and leading us inevitably to ruin. We cannot much longer continue maintaining in idleness a portion of our population, for that is the surest way to bring about communism. All our governments admit it, and the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated on the radio that he wished to abandon as soon as possible the system of direct relief, in order to undertake public works that would provide our working population with remunerative employment. It is following this speech that I conceived the idea of suggesting to the Prime Minister of my country that he contribute one million dollars towards the completion of the University of Montreal. This million dollars would be used entirely to pay wages to workers wfio
Unemployment Relief

would be taken from the ranks of the unemployed. For a few dollars more per week, we could provide our working people with employment, instead of, as at present, doling them out, thus humiliating and demoralizing charity. Direct relief is already costing millions to the federal government.
It must not be forgotten that the number of assisted persons would be doubled if every man out of work applied for relief. Fortunately for the federal treasury, our people are proud, and so long as some member of a family has some resources he uses them to assist his relatives and sometimes his friends. That is why I insist so strongly on doing away with the system of direct relief that tends to demoralize our workers and destroy their willingness to work and their initiative. It is work that we want for our labouring classes. And we want useful works that will be a credit to the country as a whole.
Is it possible to find a nobler institution to build up than a great university that could impart to our population the education necessary to the formation of competent men in all fields of our national life? The development of our higher educational system is of prime necessity to the prestige and success of our race. Consequently, we must give it all the encouragement possible. Our individual means may not be great, but our moral power is enormous and we have a right to our fair share of the national resources.
We have a right to demand that our share of these resources be applied in such a way as to do us the greatest good. If the people of Montreal and all the organized bodies in the city would unite with me in an effort to ask the Dominion government to devote a million of the relief money to the completion of the University of Montreal buildings, I am sure the government would grant that request. The more so that, if the Dominion government would grant us that money, the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal would do likewise, and we would have three millions to complete this undertaking.
Every country is proud of its universities and I am sure that, in all those who are listening to me, a patriotic chord is vibrating when I ask for a Catholic and French university that would proudly stand on the slopes of Mount Royal, for a magnificent

monument that would be an attraction for all visitors and a source of pride for all French -Canadians. But there is also the practical side: the establishment of a centre of learning that will properly develop the natural gifts of our race in all spheres of national life. I think our duty is to enrich the city of Montreal, the second largest French city in the world, with a university worthy of its high standing; and I would like to see those buildings entirely completed by the unemployed of the city, with the hope that the completion of the work will coincide with the end of the depression. And I firmly believe that, if the Dominion government decides on a rational policy of public works, it will bring peace to the minds of our people and will give to the rest of the country the confidence that is essential to put back to productive use nonactive assets, as are those of our university at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, I earnestly invite you to heed the voice of our members of parliament; I appeal to all French speaking members of my province and of the country; I urgently ask them to unite on this question, which I consider a national one, and to take the steps to have the necessary amount voted for the University of Montreal. It is an enterprise of which you all want to see the completion, and the only influence I ask for is your outspoken support. You may rest assured that my voice will then be heard in this parliament with all the more strength that I shall be speaking on behalf of three million French Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I have not very much to say in connection with this bill. I find myself in complete agreement with what was stated yesterday by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). Much as I respect him it is not very often I can agree with him on matters of policy. I must say however that I am quite in accord with everything he said about this measure. The party at present in office were elected in 1930 on a policy of ending unemployment; they gave the people of this dominion to understand that they had a solution for the problem. Generally speaking hon. members in this corner of the chamber have been very patient; as a matter of fact I believe we have been too patient. We have given the government every opportunity to fulfil its promises, and on many occasions we have offered every assistance to put into effect a program which would end unemployment.

Unemployment Reliej
Not only in 1930 but again, immediately before calling this session of parliament, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) told the people of Canada he was going to start the machinery moving which would improve conditions. Some hon. members have said they have been disappointed but I have not been disappointed because I did not expect anything. I knew very well the Prime Minister could not improve conditions without laying hands on the sacred rights of private property, and I am quite convinced he has not yet reached the point where he is willing to do that. In his last radio speech he said:
In the main I have really tried to make these business talks. To tell you the truth I am so gripped by the necessity for action, I am so anxious about the development of these reforms that I have little time to think of politics.
After giving us that very strong statement we now have dished out to us this warmed-over bill, one which we have had placed before us for the last four years. It has been warmed over each year. Some of the ingredients may be left out in the present instance, or some others may be included, but on the w:hole it is the same bill. I notice the preamble begins with the usual statement that- -the provinces may require further assistance in carrying out necessary relief measures and in meeting financial conditions as the same may arise.
There is no "may" in the matter, at all. The provinces do need assistance. The western provinces are practically bankrupt and cannot meet the obligations confronting them without the assistance of this government; and carrying on as we do I am quite convinced that even this government cannot continue much longer to carry the burden. However, until that time comes I think the government should do everything that is necessary to improve the living conditions of the people.
My colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) for comparative figures of unemployment and those on relief during the last year, and the minister replied that he did not have the figures with him at the time. However, a parliamentary return was brought down a few days ago showing the number on relief month by month from January, 1934 to January, 1935, and despite the apparent improvement which the minister told us of yesterday, according to the figures given in that return there is little dirriinution in the number of those receiving direct relief.
In the parliamentary return which I have before me I find that in January, 1934 there were 1,292,065 persons receiving direct relief, and in January of this year the number was 1,183,690, a drop of a little over 100,000. Now if you take the figures in the return you will find that since April of last year the number receiving relief decreased until the month of October, 1934, and then the number began to increase and it has increased ever since. If we take the amount of the increase in 1934 and assume that there has been a similar increase in 1935 there would have been at the end of February over 1,200,000 on direct relief. That is besides those who have been receiving relief in an indirect way, in the National Defence camps, for instance, and working on various government projects.

During the past few years the production of wealth has decreased to a very great extent, and you cannot increase taxation when the production of wealth is decreasing. The production of wealth will continue to decrease as long as markets continue to decrease. Production to-day is dependent upon the making of a profit. Markets will continue to decrease, consequently, the wealth out of which taxes are paid will also continue to decrease because the produced goods cannot be sold. No matter how much hon. friends opposite may try to improve conditions, they cannot do it under these circumstances. Mr. Chairman, could the
minister give us the total expenditures which have been made for relief by the various governments? If we are to deal effectively with unemployment in Canada we should

Unemployment Relief
give some thought to the causes of unemployment. We seem to overlook the fact that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada, and when the purchasing power of the farm people has been as low as it has been during the past four years we cannot expect anything but unemployment in the cities. We have permitted economic conditions to get out of balance. Hon. members are apt to forget the terrific drop which has occurred in the prices of farm products with the consequent decrease in the income of people living on the farms. The revenue received by the farmers of Canada represents the greatest source of purchasing power in this country. I think it is worth while to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the nbt farm income of Canada for the years 1931 to 1934 was only $1,744,000,000, as compared wih a revenue of $4,012,000,000 for the period 1926 to 1929. In four years there was a drop in purchasing power of $2,268,000,000 or fifty-seven per cent. The net revenue received by the farmers in the latter period was only forty-three per cent of what it had been in the four years preceding 1930. There was an average yearly drop of $560,000,000 in the purchasing power of the farmers of Canada. In my humble opinion this decrease in purchasing power is the chief cause of the unemployment which exists to-day. It is also the cause of the municipal debt situation. It is not that this debt has increased so much since 1929 but that we are trying to carry on with less purchasing power circulating in the hands of the people. If the government wants to deal effectively with unemployment and the situation on the farms which makes it necessary for some farmers to seek relief, they must deal directly with farm prices. These prices must be raised, and the best way of doing this is to devalue the Canadian dollar outside of Canada and bring it down until it reaches sixty-five or seventy cents in United States currency. This would bring about a rise in the level of farm prices and would prove a worth while step towards restoring prosperity on the farms, which in turn will mean more prosperity in the cities and less unemployment. Again I ask the minister if he has the total contributions made by the dominion, provincial and municipal governments to as late a date as possible?

This afternoon there was a
discussion as to the assistance the government had given to the provinces and, in turn, the provinces had given to the municipalities. I made the plea that the government should at least make some attempt to make provision whereby the municipalities might be relieved of some of the burden they are now carrying. Evidently my plea and that of other hon. members has not fallen on receptive^ ears, because only a few moments ago the minister informed the committee he hoped that when in the near future his department met with the provincial premiers there might be provision whereby the amount allotted by the government to the provinces for relief would be lower in the coming year than it has been in the past. I believe I am not far from the mark, and if I am wrong I hope the minister will correct me, when I say that the amount the government has given to the provinces and,: in turn, the provinces have remitted to the municipalities for direct relief, would amount to approximately twenty-five per cent of the expenditures. I believe I am fairly close to the mark when I say the amount would be about twenty-five per cent. In previous years the amount given by the government was one-third of the total, the provinces contributing one-third and the municipalities the remaining third. I say the additional eight and one third per cent has been carried by the municipalities, and in most cases the load is too heavy for them. I believe it is admitted on all sides that unemplojrment is not primarily a municipal problem. It is a national problem arising as a result of national conditions for which the municipalities are in no degree responsible.
Years ago, before we suffered from an acute unemployment problem, or one similar to that with which we are now faced, it was within the purview of the municipalities to grant relief to indigent cases which came under municipal control. Those indigent cases were due primarily not to problems of unemployment but rather to conditions arising out of sickness, invalidity or old age, or circumstances under which people were physically unable to find employment. However, since we have been troubled with an acute unemployment problem we find a completely new difficulty facing our municipalities, and I say we should

not expect them to carry a load ranging between thirty-five per cent and forty per cent of the cost of maintaining the unemployed. It is quite true that the problem may adjust itself; with the advent of public works and with improved economic conditions the difficulty may be lessened, but even then I say the federal government should assume its just share of the responsibility in meeting the difficulty. I am wondering whether or not the government would return to its former basis of granting relief rather than follow the practice of granting a lump sum to the provinces, not knowing whether such sum would be sufficient or insufficient to meet the necessities of the situation. I am wondering whether they would go back to the method employed prior to 1934, that of giving relief on the basis of a percentage of the cost of unemployment relief within the boundaries of the municipalities.
I am informed the province of Quebec made an offer to the government to the effect that it would asume half of the responsibility of unemployment if the federal government would assume the other half. I do not know whether any other provinces have made similar offers, but as unemployment is a national problem I do think the federal government ought to assume a much larger share of the cost than it now assumes. A few momenta ago I asked the minister if he could give the figures showing how much had been spent by way of relief to rural and urban municipalities. He was unable to give the figures, but made the statement that for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1935, approximately $32,000,000 had been spent. That figure does not convey all the information I should like to have, because some of the money was spent in the drought areas and could not be said to have been spent for the relief of the unemployed. If we had more detailed figures showing the amount actually spent we might then have some idea of what the added burden to the federal exchequer would be if the federal government assumed a larger share than it assumes at the present time. I stated earlier in my observations that the amount assumed by the federal government was approximately 25 per cent, as compared with 33j per cent in previous years. Perhaps the minister would give us the correct figures in that respect. I should also like to know if at this time he is prepared to state on behalf of the government whether or not it would grant to the municipalities more relief than they have been able to obtain from the government during the past twelve months.

The Prime Minister has once or twice said, "If we had not purchased the wheat you would not have got anything for it." I have some doubts about that and I will reserve my remarks in regard to the wheat situation until the bill comes down, when we can discuss every aspect of it.
Although I realize how useless it is, I must protest against the wide powers contained in this -bill. Ever since it has been in office this government has repeatedly come here, year
Unemployment Relief

after year, and said, "All the information we can give you is with regard to what happened last year, but we will spend any amount of money we like, in any way we like, in any place we like, when this bill is passed." In the Department of the Interior, over which I had the honour to preside, hon. gentlemen opposite when they sat over here made meticulous demands to know where every dollar would be spent, and now when the estimates for that department come down no one knows how much will be spent, in the parks, for instance. That is a right the government has taken away from parliament. My hon. friends opposite can spend any amount anywhere in the construction of roads, public buildings and so on, and parliament has no voice whatever in the matter. I cannot help thinking that hon. gentlemen opposite know just as much as we do over here about what will be done; they have not a particle more knowledge than we have. The men who constitute the government sit around a table and make these allocations as they please. I protest now, as I have protested before and will continue to protest, against this method. It may be necessary to have unidentified sums voted for the purpose of assisting the provinces, but there is certainly no excuse on earth that I can think of for the expenditure of public money in the parks under the guise of relief without having that money voted, as it has always been voted in the past, thereby preserving the rights of parliament in .the matter. And the same applies to every other expenditure of public money on undertakings which the government itself is carrying out; they should be separated from this act. If there is any excuse on earth for this bill it can only be the fact that my hon. friends do not know how much they will spend in conjunction with the provinces, but there is no excuse whatever for including in the bill the right of the government to make expenditures over which they have complete control, without the money being voted. There is not much use protesting, however. Our good friends say it is remarkable that the Liberal party should be agreeing with the Conservative party in all these matters of social reform now being passed. What is the use of protesting? My hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) has just remarked that he voted for the bill this afternoon-I was not here-on the ground that it contained a provision for continuing cooperative marketing. Well, he need not have worried because the government own the wheat and will have to sell it. They are bringing down a bill under 
which they will operate next year-I fancy that will be the effect of it-and if he objects to the rest of the bill I do not see that there was much necessity for his voting for the bill to continue the wheat operations seeing that the government of Canada practically speaking own all the wheat now. However I want to make it quite plain that I am. protesting as strongly as I can against the practice that has been followed by this government, without letting us know the details as to. place or anything else, or spending public money in the way that has been done. Possibly they do not know themselves, though they should know. All we know is that the returns come in as provided for under the act and we are so informed when parliament meets. Talk about autocracy: we have it in the fullest measure year by year, and again this year in the particular bill which we are now discussing.

I know in my riding at least one municipality which is unable to pay a single cent for the purpose of relieving the unemployed. This municipality, a small one, was living by the taxes of workers in the brick industry. Since 1930 those brick plants have been idle and at least a hundred families are practically in a State of starvation. They are all small, humble proprietors and consequently unable to pay their taxes, and the municipality is- I hate to use the word "bankrupt"-really unable to provide the money to come to their rescue. The minister is in a better position than I am to know how many municipalities throughout Canada are in a similar situation. Oh yes, but that is an old story. To come down to modem history, to the number of unemployed at the present time and their classification by trade or profession, it is very easy to gather that information, and
if there is to be an interprovincial conference this important question should be brought before the provinces in order that the country may be well posted on it. May I say to the minister that prominent members of the St. Vincent de Paul Society have told me that the information could be secured within twenty-four hours, that it was there and had only to be compiled. That information could also be secured, not through trades unions, but by charitable organizations like the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, and the St. Vincent de Paul Society which I have already mentioned. Therefore in the interests of the country I now ask the Minister of Labour to take due steps to have the unemployed classified. It would serve the government well because as soon as that classification is made the governments, whether federal or provincial does not matter, and I use the plural intentionally, will be able to distinguish between those who are really unemployed and those who take advantage of relief in order to get assistance to which they are not entitled. The saving of money thus made would compensate for any expense that might be incurred in making such a classification. I cannot close my brief remarks without thanking the minister for his answer. It has taken me a long time, five years, to get that answer from him, but at last to-night I have got it, and I am satisfied he is now on the right path and I hope he will continue in it.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Morand in the chair.
Miscellaneous-
To assist in promoting tourist business in Canada, $200,000.

Before this vote is carried I should like to say a few words, and first of all I should like to congratulate the Minister of Railways upon his very able presentation of the case for Canada as a country offering many attractions to the outside tourist. I think the whole country owes a debt of gratitude to Hon. Mr Dennis, Senator from Halifax, because it was upon his initiative that the Senate appointed a special committee last session to inquire into the possibilities of the tourist traffic and to ascertain what steps could be taken to encourage and develop this traffic. As a result
Supply-Railways-Tourists

of the work of that committee a publicity department was established, from which excellent results are to be expected.
Among the facts brought out by the committee was that in 1929, the last year in which good times prevailed in the United States, Canada received a revenue of $310,000,000 from the outside tourist trade. Those who have made a study of this matter anticipate that when times once more become normal the trade will provide a revenue of $500,000,000. I think that this is the opportune time to make a special drive for this trade. It is said that 20,000/300 people visited the Chicago fair in 1933, with possibly a like number in 1934. It is natural to expect that many of these people will be looking for a new place in which to spend their vacation this year, and there is no country with the attractions of Canada. If a special drive is made immediately we could expect a large share of this trade. The whole dominion is interested in this question, but Ontario is particularly interested because of its proximity to the more populous centres of the United States. In addition our province has the added advantage of good roads and easy access by rail and water.
There is no trade or industry-I think we can call it that-which provides such general and in some cases generous benefits. Practically all classes of the community receive benefits from this trade. The hotel keeper, the boarding house keeper, the merchant, the garage man, the mechanic, the cook, the guide, the boat livery man, the farmer and the market gardener all receive direct benefits from this trade, and through them the benefits are spread to all classes in the community. Large sums of money have been spent upon our railroads and highways, and if this tourist traffic is encouraged we will be able to obtain some return on our investment. Those who have spoken before me on this question have laid before the house some of the special attractions which their particular province or constituency possesses, and perhaps I may be allowed to do the same thing.
I consider that my riding of East Simcoe possesses unique advantages because of its history and scenery. The history of this riding goes back to 1615 when Champlain, that great adventurer from France, journeyed up the Ottawa river, passed into lake Nipis-sing, came out into Georgian bay, then down to Penetanguishene, finally landing at Orillia. He wintered there in anticipation of joining the Huron Indians on a warlike expedition against the Iroquois. Through the public spirit which is characteristic of them, the

citizens of Orillia have erected a monument to the memory of Champlain which is said to be the finest of its kind in Canada. This was made possible only after a considerable expenditure of time and money, aided by contributions from the dominion, Ontario and Quebec governments. Every year thousands of tourists from Canada and the United States visit Orillia in order to view this monument.
I suggest to the minister that in any publicity issued in connection with the tourist traffic particular mention should be made of this monument.
Adjacent to the town of Midland is a martyr's shrine erected to the memory of those heroic Jesuit missionaries, Fathers Brebeuf and Lallemant, who were taken captive by the Iroquois and so cruelly tortured to death. This shrine is a most attractive spot for tourists from Ontario, Quebec and the United States, and I think it should be emphasized in any publicity which is issued.
Penetanguishene celebrated its tercentenary in 1919, a delay of four years having occurred because of the war. The chiefs of the Huron and Iroquois tribes were invited to be present, and they met and smoked the pipe of peace and entered into what is hoped will be a lasting treaty. During the war of 1812 Penetanguishene was selected as the proper place for the establishment of a naval and military station. At the conclusion of the war the American war vessels Tigress and Scorpion, which were captured from the Americans at Mackinaw, were sunk. Recently one of them has been brought to the surface and provides an object of great interest to American tourists. So much for the historic points in my riding.
I shall deal now with the points of special scenic beauty. My riding lies at the gateway of the thirty thousand islands of the Georgian bay. This area has recently been made a national park by the dominion government. The trip from Midland to Parry Sound through the inside channel is said to be the finest trip of its kind in Canada. I suggest to hon. members that if they want to see something of the beauties of Ontario they should take that trip. In addition to the wonderful trip among the thirty thousand islands we have the Severn river which forms the northern link of the Trent waterways connecting Georgian bay with lake Couchiching. Thousands of tourists spend the summer there and there is room for thousands more. I have mentioned briefly a few of the attractive points in my riding and I am sure I voice the views of my constituency when I say that we are heartily in favour of this vote.

I would not consider it necessary to speak but for the fact that the people I represent are very much interested in the tourist traffic. The county of Peterborough offers a great deal of attraction to tourists who come by thousands to enjoy the scenery. We are able to give them and we do give them a very pleasant time and they come again. I agree with my hon. friend from East Simcoe as to the attractiveness of that general system that runs from Georgian bay to the Trent, known as the Kawartha system, comprising islands, lakes, rivers and canals. It attracts many thousands of people to its shores every year and those whom I represent are particularly interested in promoting the traffic. Other places in Canada are similarly situated and are looking for tourists. I am quite sure therefore that the government is doing the wise thing in setting aside a sum of money to advertise the traffic and to make provision for tourists to see that they are properly guarded against exorbitant charges. The bureau can do a great deal in furnishing information to the prospective tourist. After all, the best advertisement that Canada can have is the good will of those who visit the country and report favourably upon its advantages. That is the first essential. Further, the bureau should be in a position to give information to those who are ignorant of the country and are anxious to know where they can spend a happy and profitable holiday at reasonable cost. It will be the function of the bureau to collect all this information and to check it over, and it can do many things to smooth the way for the tourist. The tourist wants a reasonable means of approaching the particular point on which he has set his mind; he wants to know that he will be comfortably looked after at moderate cost; he wants to know that fishing is provided for, and he wants to know particularly that he will be able to get into ready communication with his own home by mail, telegraph or telephone. A good many inquiries are made respecting the district I come from with regard to these points particularly which I have enumerated, and the officer in charge of the bureau can do a good deal in cooperation with the various departments to clear up such points. Every man coming to visit us wants to know, as I have said, that he will be able to get into ready communication with his home in case of emergency. From every point of view therefore we can commend this appropriation and I congratulate the government. I assure them it will do a great deal to improve the tourist traffic and increase the numbers of those who visit us.

Before the house rose a few days ago I mentioned the great buffalo park situated between Wainwright and Har-disty in Alberta. There are a few particulars which I wish to put on record with regard to this park, which has the reputation of being the largest buffalo park with the largest herd of buffalo in the world. The park is situated on the main line of the Canadian National railways, 127 miles east of Edmonton and 199 miles west of Saskatoon. It has an area of 125,000 acres. The buffalo were first introduced into the park in 1910, and the locality being exceedingly good for them, and great care having been taken of them, they have increased enormously; from 748 they have increased to 24,000. Various means have been taken to keep the herd within reasonable numbers owing to the limited pasture. In the years from 1925 to 1928 no less than 6,673 were moved north to the Wood Buffalo park in the Great Slave lake region, and during recent years a great number of the older animals have been slaughtered-to be exact, 10,545. We still have approximately 5,000 in t)he park. Besides buffalo we have 1,000 head of elk, 2,500 mule deer, 95 moose and a small herd of yak. There are many interesting crosses between the buffalo, the yak and the domestic, which are of considerable interest to visitors. Last year visitors to the park numbered 12,631. The park is surrounded by a high wire fence, nine feet high, stretching for over one hundred miles. I am glad to say that we have at Wainwright Park a very able administrator in Mr. Smith, who goes to a great deal of trouble to give every consideration to visitors. I want to put these facts on record because I think the parks should be advertised more extensively. I believe that the money being spent by the government in advertising these different parks is all to the good. Apart from the park there is another attraction in the Wainwright area, where we have the second largest oil field in Canada, so that if people get tired looking at the buffalo they can look at possible investments in this important oil field.

There has been such unanimity with regard to this appropriation that I hesitate to take up the time of the committee, but it would be most unusual and neglectful if on such a discussion as this the province of Nova Scotia were 'overlooked. That province is the playground of the Atlantic, and the constituency which I have the honour to represent is from the tourist standpoint the chief asset of that province. In addition to the attractions that should be held out to tourists

and that have been mentioned by the minister and also by the hon. member for East Simcoe; in addition to the courtesy, kindness and hospitality that should be shown to tourists, there should be attractions in the shape of good roads, hotels and tourist camps which also should be developed.
The hon. member for East Simcoe in his very worthy address referred to the historic aspects of his constituency. Well, the tourist that comes to Nova Scotia in nine cases out of ten wishes to see the one historic point in Canada that is probably more important than any other, and that is the old town of Louisburg. They read about it in their schoolbooks many years ago, and as the years went on their interest no doubt grew. Perhaps as they took a deeper interest in Canadian history they got a better view and a keener realization of the importance of the fall of Louisburg in 1758. At that time Louisburg was the key to the gulf of St. Lawrence; the taking of that town meant the taking of the French citadel on the Atlantic coast. The following year the British were enabled to make Louisburg a strategic point from which to take Quebec. Had it not been for the capture of Louisburg in 1758, it would have been very difficult if not impossible to take Quebec the following year, and thus students of history recognize that in that old town was fought out and probably settled the destiny of Canada and probably of the whole North American continent for all time to come.
I admire the efforts of hon. members who have already spoken in praise of the beauties of their various constituencies, but I wonder what would happen to them and to their point of view if they visited the province of Nova Scotia and the county of Cape Breton There is where the east begins; there is where the sun first kisses the eastern shore of Canada, and I venture to say that in the course of its long journey until it sets in the waters of the Pacific it does not look upon a more beautiful scene than that which greets it at dawn in Nova Scotia.
I wish I could induce some hon. members to visit the island of Cape Breton and take just a short trip around it. The first spot I would take them to would be the village of Margaree, where is possibly the most fertile valley in the eastern provinces. There is to be found the celebrated Margaree river, the paradise of the angler, where salmon and trout abound and where the greatest hospitality is extended to the tourist. The tourist after a few days' visit there goes home
{Mr. F. MacDonald.]
satisfied with the treatment he has received, with the fish he has caught and probably with material enough to furnish conversation for many a long evening. From there I would take him along the celebrated Cabot trail over the tip of Cape North, up the side of a mountain the size of which is such that it makes even the Alps and the Rocky mountains dwindle, and on which cars go in low gear until they reach the top. From that point of vantage you can see in the distance Prince Edward Island, the garden of the gulf, so described by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers) the other day'. Turning your gaze to the right you see the distant shores of Newfoundland, then down the Atlantic coast over the mountain of Smoky is the village of Baddeck, made prominent many years ago by Charles W. Warner, and now the resting place of Alexander Graham Bell, the great inventor, who having travelled over the world picked this spot as one of the most beautiful he had ever seen. It was there that the first aeroplanes flew in the Dominion of Canada, and there opens to the eyes of the public the beauty of the great Bras d'Or lakes. A little further on we come to the village of St. Ann's, the birthplace and resting place of the celebrated giant McAskill.
When hon. members who speak of the attractions of their constituencies refer to fishing such as is afforded by the lakes of Ontario and other small spots, they are speaking simply of minor league fish. If they want to have big league fish they have to come down to Cape Breton island. There we have a fish called the tuna, a member of the horse mackerel family. I might read just one short description of it:
In no other waters of the world are there found so many world champion heavyweight deep sea fighters and few with so abundant a variety of lightweight sport fish. They range along the south shore and off Cape Breton. Nova Scotia tuna-the battling giants of the sea! The biggest thrill awaiting those who find their sport with rod and line! The gamest and most enduring fighters in the ocean are the tuna found in Nova Scotian waters.
